utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: H denotes the distance between the tip of the shell, the unexploded shell - it's very well known, measured very precisely - and point C, which is the center of explosion. The center of explosion is, in fact, the center of the mass of the explosive charge of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is the source of your measurement of the letter H?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: The source is the extensive literature we had available to us. Sarajevo was one of the centres of military industry, and there is a voluminous literature containing all the details of explosive devices that we had before and still have, and we had it in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, as a general matter, the cosine of an angle is the ratio of the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse; is that right? I'm sorry, that should be the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Precisely, and the cosinus of the angle is a nameless number, it's 03417.45, but the angle, itself, is the inverse of that number. Alpha is the arc cosinus of that number, and here it's calculated as 70.01 degrees. I think it's important to mention one thing here: The calculation relevant to this picture we're looking at does not have a single incoming datum nor anything in common with the previous calculation where we're calculating the minimum possible angle of descent relative to the height of the building. This calculation was done absolutely independently of the other calculation and relied on the traces on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The angle of 70.01 degrees is equivalent to an angle of 1166.67, using the other measurement system; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Precisely. But mathematically, these are the same angles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your previous evidence, you marked in red some features of this. I want to focus just on the two arrows marked with the letters L and R. Could you describe the pattern of distribution of shrapnel at the moment of detonation of a 120-millimetre mortar projectile?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: As briefly as possible, the greatest density of the shrapnel and the highest force of the explosion goes in the direction marked as L and R. In this case, I will only recall the injuries to the lower extremities; the torn feet, heels, and parts of the foot. And at the other extreme is the man who was hanging over a rail, who was hurt in the chest. This explains that victims to the north of the impact were hurt in the upper part of the body. So apart from body parts, we saw brains spilling out and other injuries. That was at the L direction. And in the opposite direction was the line R, and causing completely different injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I request that that be admitted, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1928, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in respect of the Markale 2 incident, you also determined the direction of fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's one of the most important parameters for determining the origin of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I want to clarify clearly. Were you able to determine the precise distance travelled by a projectile before the moment of impact?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: No, we did not manage to do that because we didn't know with how many charges the projectile was launched. However, many facts indicate that this projectile was launched with three plus zero charges, which is an approximate distance of 2400 metres, perhaps 2500 metres, but the exact place could only be determined by observers or by acoustic sensors or by radar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to 65 ter 10222, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you recall the conclusion you came to regarding the direction of fire of the projectile in the Markale 2 incident?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the azimuth, 170. In the attempt to establish the azimuth as correctly as possible and to exclude the subjective factor, which cannot be avoided, all members of our team determined this direction independently one of another, and then we compared our measurements. Now, 15 years after the incident, even though I was certain of the direction then, I am even more certain now, after having read all the reports by the UN observers and other experts who confirmed the angle that we arrived at by very precise analysis. I'm not saying it's our angle; I'm saying that the angle we determined is very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And on the screen in front of you, we see a line pointing towards a figure of 170. Is that the direction of fire of the projectile in this incident?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. We wrote in the report "170 degrees plus/minus 5 degrees," as the allowed error of margin, accounting for subjectivity or, perhaps, inclarities [as interpreted] on the ground. That's the standard error margin assigned to an angle that we believe to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you explain - you can use a pen if you want to - why did you exclude a possibility of there being a direction of fire of 220 degrees?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask that, for my benefit and that of the other witnesses who come here, this screen be turned a little sideways towards me, because the light reflects from the ceiling and I can't see so well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher can assist the witness with the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, I'll manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: There's no need to mark the screen, unless you have to. I just want to you explain --

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: It's fine, it's fine. It's all right, there's no need. But on one picture, I saw much more clearly, in this part that I'm marking now [marks], an extended wing of the trace of this shrapnel, which confirms the assertion that the azimuth was 170 degrees. I believe these scars of the shrapnel was stained over by blood on that photograph, and that's why I want to clarify this here. But on the spot, we did not have that dilemma, because when you are looking at the real thing, it's much clearer than a photograph can reproduce. You have, among your documentation, one picture that shows the traces of these shrapnel that I tried to hint at with these blue lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. We'll try to get that photograph. But could you explain, briefly, your reasons for excluding the possibility of an angle -- a direction of fire of 220 degrees?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. If you speculate with an angle of 220, and some reports even play with an interval of between 220 and 240, that means that there would have to be a so-called "eyebrow-shaped" line showing the spread of the shrapnel towards dotted line G, in relation to which the vertical would be -- would form this angle of 220. Since left of the explosion, this line here -- this other line here has no base -- has no traces of shrapnel towards this G line, I believe that a 220 angle is absolutely out of the question as azimuth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to bring up now the file of photographs which you looked at earlier, which is 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to tender this one, as marked?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And for the record, I wanted to make sure that the markings already on the picture is done by the witness in previous cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. This is part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you confirmed that with the witness, that this is part of the associated exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps, Witness, could you sign and date this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: [In English] What is the date today, the 11th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it it's the 4th of November, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Both versions will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the previously-marked version will be Exhibit P1929, and the annotations made today will be Exhibit P1930.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we could bring up the previous file of photographs, which is 09900.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if we go to photograph 7 now of this, please. Does that photograph assist your recollection at all?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Those traces of shrapnel that I just hinted at with the blue fields on the previous picture are now visible on the left. Looking from the place where the shell landed, to the left. Is it necessary to mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, I think it would be clearest if you marked that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zoom out, please, zoom out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you touch the screen, you may need to push some button. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you mark the area that you were talking about earlier and explain the point that you were making.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. [Interpretation] These are the shrapnel traces that are now between and inside these blue lines, that are hardly visible on the previous picture, where I indicated they should be, because I saw them in another picture. However, when we were determining the azimuth in the flesh, so to speak, we saw these traces, and we acknowledged their symmetry to determine the azimuth correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you sign and date that photograph, please, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And could I tender that, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put your signature and date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as P1931.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, my final couple of questions, Witness: Could you tell the Court, in a general manner, in respect of how many incidents where you were a participant in the investigations did you personally visit the scene of the incident?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: This is very hard to say, because we never kept statistics of our activities. But from my recollection, it was at least 100 scenes where I participated directly, and perhaps as many more where I participated as a consultant. And our team was the most responsible for such cases, while consulting as many colleagues as possible, in the fields of their expertise, to take into account as many facts as possible in every investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In all those investigations that you participated in, did you ever encounter credible information suggesting that Bosnian Government forces were deliberately targeting civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That ends the direct examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps I should deal with the associated exhibits at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In our notification, we pointed out two exhibits which have previously been admitted. I'd now like to point out that one further exhibit has been admitted through the witness who testified earlier. 65 ter 09906 has been admitted as P1908 in the public redacted version and P1909 as the original version under seal. And I tender for the admission of the rest of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly name those two exhibits that have been already admitted again? I note one 09867?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I'll just get my copy of the notification. Bear with me for one moment, please. Yes, Mr. President, 09786 has been admitted as P1324, and 09867 has been admitted as P1336.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Yes, all the others will be admitted and given numbers by the Court Deputy. Thank you. Before you start your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic, Judge Morrison has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Turkusic, you said, in answer to one of the questions from the Prosecution -- or gave a statement as to what your views were as to the policy or reasoning behind the incident we've been dealing with, and to paraphrase it, that it was, in your view, done in order to cause fear amongst the population and to drive their political leaders into negotiation, or words to that general effect. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Now, would you agree that those are your personal views that you have formed as a result of your own experiences and observations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not agree, because my opinion is shared by a huge number of people who have gone through the inferno of Sarajevo and bore witness to the fact that in all the places where the shells fell, there were only civilian targets, that air-bombs fell on the most densely-populated part of Sarajevo, Alipasino Polje, a bomb of 300 kilos is falling on a neighbourhood full of high-rises where the density of population is the greatest. What else could it be except intention to intimidate, sow fear and panic, and pressurise our leadership to be more pliable and more accepting, whatever that means?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No doubt there may be a great many people who share your views, but I want to concentrate on your views. You may share your views with a lot of people, but your views are, of course, your personal subjective views, formed as a result of your own experiences and observations. Other people may have similar views, but those are your views, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I would add to my explanation just one fact. It's well known that very frequently, after firing one shell, another was fired five minutes later onto the same place. It's well known that when many people gather to help the victims, that again is a good target for shelling, and these people are the object -- the target of the second shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And the thrust of your evidence is to provide the scientific and mathematical calculation and crater analysis to determine where this particular shell came from; that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it seems to the Bench that the views of the witness have been made plain, but your task is not to, as it were, examine those views, but to concentrate on the scientific and mathematical calculations and the crater analysis which has led this witness to the conclusions that he has made and from which other conclusions may flow. So rather than embarking upon a political analysis of his views, concentrate on a scientific analysis and cross-examination of his findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I propose to take a break now. We'll have a break for an hour, so we'll resume at 10 to 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 11.50 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Karadzic starts his cross-examination, there are a couple of matters I would like to deal with. The first thing is I'd like to revisit the issue of admission of associated exhibits. Mr. Gaynor, amongst the exhibits, associated exhibits, are there any reports which relate to unscheduled incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, there are, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you identify them now for our purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. The incident at -- well, 21611 is the incident at Bolnicka Street 25. 21628 is the incident at Baruthana Street number 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The 65 ter number, 21 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry. The second one is 21628.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 21628. And the first one was ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The third one is 09867.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 098 -- could you give it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: 09867. The next one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, as P1336. The next one is 21629.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next one is 21632.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: 21625, 21636, 21635. Now, there are Exhibit -- sorry, 65 ter 16835 concerns two of the shells which fell around the same time as the Markale 2 shell. So, in a sense, they are associated with that incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gaynor, do you remember that the Chamber has stated previously that it would not admit detailed evidence going to unscheduled incidents, including those incidents that had been included in the schedule, and in relation to which evidence should no longer be presented pursuant to Rule 73 bis (D)?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I recall the Chamber's ruling, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So upon reflection and to ensure consistency with our previous rulings, the Judges have decided to partially reconsider this earlier decision, admitting those associated exhibits in relation to the unscheduled incidents. So the Chamber has decided to reconsider our decision to admit those associated exhibits, which are Bosnian Muslim reports on various unscheduled incidents. I take it there are 12 or 11, excluding the Markale 2 incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the reason for this is that it will be -- we are going to take steps, whenever we can, to make this case more manageable. So if you -- since these reports are not admitted into evidence, I will give you an opportunity, if you so wish, to go through, in a very general manner, in relation to those unscheduled incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: With the witness in direct examination? Yes, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you so wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to do that, Mr. President, for one particular reason, and that is the reports indicate the markings on the stabiliser fin in the -- on the projectiles in respect of many of those incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Except those you went through with the witness in your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. In respect of many of the unscheduled incidents which weren't discussed in direct examination, the reports state that the stabilisers contain markings showing that they were manufactured in Krusik Valjevo, in Serbia. And then tying in with other evidence in the Prosecution case, those stabilisers were then transported to VRS troops within Bosnia to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. So this evidence -- the point I'm making, Mr. President, is that this evidence goes beyond merely proving the scheduled incidents; it goes to showing the provenance of the projectiles and goes towards our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you wish, you may go through the topics with the witness in the second direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll do that now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Thank you very much for that ruling. I was actually biting my tongue not to be objecting to unscheduled incidents, which seemed to be something that we agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To the understanding, to the understanding of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. But following up on that, the amalgamated statement contains a lot of information about unscheduled incidents that ought to be redacted, consistent with your ruling, including some conclusions that the shell had been fired from the area under the control of the aggressor; for example, in item 8 on page 10. So if the idea is to save time, I think that we should also redact the amalgamated statement so that it doesn't contain any information about unscheduled incidents, and then leave it to Mr. Gaynor to decide how much he wants to try to elicit, and leave it to the Chamber as to how much you want to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any response, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No. Your Honours have previously given a ruling as to the admissibility of evidence going to unscheduled incidents, generally, related to a widespread and systematic nature of the attack on the civilian population and the existence of a campaign of shelling and sniping, so I don't believe that Mr. Robinson's submission is consistent with that ruling by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You would like to comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. If this was a jury trial, Mr. Robinson, there would be every reason to redact it from material that was going before the jury. You'll have to trust that redaction is a mental process, as far as a chamber which has judges of both fact and law. We've already seen this material in the statement, anyway, so simply physically redacting it from the document is not going to make a material difference. It's a mental redaction that's required, and you can rest assured that that will happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that, but actually a 92 ter statement is part of the evidence as if it was direct examination. It can be used in the judgement. So if the idea is to stop -- not spend a lot of time on these incidents, the fact that they are contained in the 92 ter statement, regardless of their influence on you, compels us, I think, or gives us at least the obligation to deal with those incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, what we allowed is a general overview -- a general analysis in relation to the unscheduled incidents. What we decided to avoid is a detailed analysis into it. So I think, for example, the Prosecution's asked the witness, Based upon his experience and investigation, you have a general overview about these incidents. He can answer whatever he likes to. And the statements reflected in the statement fits to that general description.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. President. However, I don't think that would solve our problem cross-examining on the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you know the ruling of the Chamber to allow the Prosecution to lead evidence, in a general manner, on unscheduled incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but I don't see how we're going to save a lot of time in cross-examination if the material in the amalgamated statement remains. But, anyway, we can cross that bridge when we welcome to it. I understand your ruling, and I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. So I'll now go briefly through the documents in question, Mr. President. Could I ask for 21624, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The document coming up, Mr. Turkusic, if we look on the second page of the document in the original version, we see at the bottom of the second page the signature of Mirza Jamakovic and, to the left of that, the letters "ET." Could you confirm what the letters "ET" mean?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: These are my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does that mean that you drafted this report?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, a little bit above your signature, we see a reference to a marking on the stabiliser, and the marking is "MK M74 KB 9309." Could you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That indicates the type of the weapon or the shell. The "KV" and "9309," that means that the fuse and the stabiliser of the shell was produced in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The letters which are "KB" on the shell, is that the Cyrillic equivalent of the Latin letters "KV"?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And we see your conclusion concerning the direction of fire and your conclusion that the projectile had been fired from the area in the direction of Grdonj and Mrkovici. Could you just explain briefly how you came to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I would just like to object -- maybe I misunderstood your ruling, but I thought you didn't want to go into this level of detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. I'll simply go through the documents slightly faster. Is that what you wish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was mistaken. You are on 65 ter 21624?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is also related to an unscheduled incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, this is the first unscheduled incident. It's on page 7 of the amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without going into the detail of the reports, can you cover the unscheduled incidents in general terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what I intended. I thought that was -- that was the report on one of the scheduled incidents. I was mistaken. But what I wanted you to do is to cover the unscheduled incident without relying on these reports. Just go through in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The whole purpose is to show the pattern or the systematic nature or the widespread nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Gaynor. Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I'm waiting for the interpretation. May I ask something? If I know and see that this is an error, that it was incorrectly established, and if this is part of the case file, and if it can have an effect on the final outcome, on the judgement, do I have the right to dispute every single detail of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You do. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you also participated in the investigation of a shelling at Bolnicka Street number 25 on the 26th of May, 1995; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please show me the material just so that I can refresh my recollection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 21611, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection of this investigation?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were given a request from the Sarajevo CSB to analyse, and it says that: "The following material is submitted for expert opinion -- the following material collected at the crime scene was submitted for expert analysis: Fragment of the projectile with wings, 10 metal fragments of the irregular shape," and then the rest is illegible. Perhaps we can zoom in a little bit. I think it says "calibre of the projectile," but it's a bit indistinct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the translation in English is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down a little bit more in the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene, interfere with you so many times, but there seems to be a misunderstanding. I just quickly went through his amalgamated statement again right now, and it really contains, albeit briefly, the elements -- the evidence contains the elements of unscheduled incidents, i.e., the date and time, calibre or -- calibre, and the markings, and where they are from, and also there is some evidence about the direction or azimuth. So I'm wondering whether you need to go through them again. I said if you so wish, given that we are not admitting those reports, you may go through quickly, but I didn't say you have to. It's up to you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour's point. Apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think the material points of each report are reflected in the amalgamated statement; and in that case, there's no need to question the witness about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wasn't clear enough. Before you start your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic, Judge Baird has a word for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I would like to make an addendum to what Judge Morrison told you before the break. We were offering advice; nothing more, nothing less. This must not be construed in any way as being any sort of restriction that we are imposing on what you should or what you should not cross-examine. Obviously, if you asked a question that is irrelevant, it wouldn't be allowed, but we are not prohibiting you in any way from cross-examining in the manner you see fit. Well, as long, of course, as it is within the bounds of propriety. You have the conduct of your defence. What is your defence, you have, in pectore, and you, and you alone, would decide the form your cross-examination would take. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I hope that through this reconsideration exercise, the parties are fully aware of the Chamber's concerns regarding the scope of the case, and I think this reconsideration is one step in this regard. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In line with the spirit of Your Honour's ruling, can I just ask one or two additional questions of the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Turkusic, in your statement, you've described investigations into a number of incidents in which markings were contained on the stabiliser, indicating that they'd been manufactured in Krusik Valjevo in Serbia. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do; not only Krusik Valjevo in Serbia, but also during the war, and this is important to know as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And is this merely a selection of the incidents which you investigated in which you found stabilisers with markings suggesting that the stabiliser had been manufactured in Krusik Valjevo?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I, personally, wasn't able to have any influence on the selection of cases. After the war, those who participated in the investigations here came to Sarajevo. They copied the entire documentation. And then the selection made by the OTP was something that was presented to me, and I gave my answers on the basis of that. We didn't make any selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could you -- you've anticipated my point. But the reports which you've reviewed are merely an illustrative set of examples of investigations into incidents where the projectile bore markings suggesting that the stabiliser had been manufactured in Krusik Valjevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, generally speaking, concerning the targets of incidents which you investigated, could you give the Court an overall impression whether the targets of the incidents which you investigated were primarily civilian or primarily of a military nature? Could you clarify that for the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: These were predominantly civilian targets; residential homes, hospitals, schools, kindergartens. They were all predominantly civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. Dr. Turkusic, probably you heard this from the VWS, but I'd like to remind you once again. Because Mr. Karadzic and you are speaking the same language, you need to put a pause between the question and answer in order for the interpreters to follow you. So if you are starting your answer -- giving your answer before the interpretation is over, because of the overlapping, they can't hear you answering. So please bear that in mind. One option for you is to look at the transcript, and if it stops, then you can start your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. First of all, I would like to thank Your Excellencies Morrison and Baird for this encouragement and for the useful suggestions. What I am concerned about is the ambition of the Prosecutor to introduce technical data --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I wanted to say is that I have 15 minutes per incident. This is what I wanted to say. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Turkusic.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would just briefly and, if possible, with as many yes-or-no answers as possible, to cover with you as many matters as possible so that both of us could go home as soon as possible, especially you. Can you please tell me: Which party were you a member of in the elections of 1990 and after 1990?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I didn't belong to any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the beginning of the war, you were a volunteer or you were mobilised in the 1st Dobrinja Brigade; what is correct of that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Volunteer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put a pause. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, how many brigades were there in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Because of my intervention, probably, your answer was not correctly reflected. What did you say to the previous question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I voluntarily joined the 1st Dobrinja Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us: How many brigades were there in Dobrinja in the beginning? This was the 1st. How many more were there?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: The first one and the only one. I don't know of any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that it was later renamed as the 5th Motorised and then later the 155th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that corresponds to the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And which battalion were you in?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I wasn't in any battalion. I wasn't in any battalion but in a sector that dealt with the same things that I later dealt with in the KDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were in the HQ of the brigade, in a way, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: It's a well-known name. I frequently hear of that name in the streets of Sarajevo, but, actually, right now I cannot remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many battalions did the brigade have?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I have no information about that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was its HQ?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: The HQ was in the ground floor and the cellar of a building in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the address?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was exactly the work you were doing there? Were you dealing with weapons? What was the work you were focused on as part of your regular duties?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: The group -- I, myself, and the group that I described were disarming or de-mining unexploded shells. Thank God there were such shells. We would extract explosives from some of them and provide it for further use in defence, because we were the only ones subjected to the embargo of all the armies that were waging war then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am astonished to hear that there were many unexploded shells. Can you tell us: Which were the ones which most frequently failed to explode?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: In the literature worldwide, there is statistics about unexploded shells, and it ranges in the amount of a couple of percentages, which depends on the angle of descent and ricochets. There were cumulative-charge shells, which are quite easily deactivated, as well as mortar shells. However, if, out of a thousand grenades, shells, you've got 4 per cent unexploded, that's 40, so that would be quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So 4 per cent. But out of these shells, were some more prone to failures than others?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I don't have the requisite knowledge to be able to either confirm or deny the statement in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I can see that you were also involved in the manufacture of arms, and you used explosives. What is it that one can put to use out of a shell?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, quite a few things. Number 1, explosives, which is most frequently the TNT, which is harmless to handle, because it can basically melt out of an unexploded shell through vapour or can be hammered out of a shell. If I compare the TNT to the candle wax, then I think that it will make things much clearer to everyone, because the material is quite similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In some of your material, you say that you produced shells and even rifles. Could the body of the shell be put to any use? And if so, which use was it put to?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I don't have that sort of information. I don't have information to the effect that ever a body of an unexploded shell was reused, or the casing. And you also said that I manufactured rifles. That's not true. I don't know where you got that information from. I never stated anything of the sort in relation to rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that most of the shells were manufactured in towns across Bosnia-Herzegovina and that Bosnia-Herzegovina had capable personnel to manufacture the weapons. And this was stated by you in Perisic on the 21st January 2009 at page 2775. This is for the benefit of everyone in the courtroom. Is this what you stated?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about Bosnia, it is common knowledge that there were several locations in Bosnia which produced weapons, which meant that they had to have highly qualified and professional cadre to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you, for the benefit of Their Honours, briefly enumerate the various companies dealing with special-purpose industry in Bosnia and Herzegovina and under whose control they were during the war.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Before the war, the highest manufacturing capacity was by the Pretis factory in Vogosca, which I think was the highest manufacturing capacity of artillery pieces in the entire Yugoslavia. That's my view. Right at the outset of the war, we weren't able to control either the location or its production, and I'm talking about Pretis. I know that there was another industrial plant in Bugojno producing ammunition, as well as in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Novi Travnik; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was there -- what was produced there? Cannons, I believe.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What sort of shells were produced by Pretis?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Cannon shells, Howitzer shells, and, I believe, mortar shells, if I remember correctly, because for many years before the war, large amounts of such shells were laid out in the industrial grounds surrounding the plant. They would be transported by forklifts from one stage of manufacturer plant to another. So this was the largest industrial plant of the sort which, right at the start of the war, the Serbs placed under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you also agree that air-bombs were produced there?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have information to that effect. According to what I know, air-bombs were repaired in Serbia or Montenegro, perhaps in Tivat. They were repaired and serviced there and made ready for use. They were subsequently used in ways you are better familiar with than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that of the various military, economic, and political centres, Bihac, Tuzla, Zenica and down-town Sarajevo remained under the control of the Muslim-Croat coalition, i.e., federation?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of a Muslim-Croat coalition. I don't know who you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I mean the BH Federation, which was first called [indiscernible] the Dayton Accords, but let's leave it at that. Did these not remain under the control of the BH Federation?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: You mean these towns? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in Tito's era, industry and stocks were spread out and stored across Yugoslavia in the event of an attack, for the eventuality of an attack?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: The complete arsenal and stockpiles were, before the war, placed fully under the control of the then Yugoslav People's Army. Now, the ammunition and weapons held by the Territorial Defence were, shortly before the war, also placed under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army, which, in practice, meant a full disarmament of Bosnia-Herzegovina before embargo was imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll deal with this matter with someone else, but I do claim that huge stockpiles of weapons, like those in Zenica, remained where they were. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I would very much like the case -- this to be the case, but this was not the case. Republika Srpska had under their full control all of the weapons and ammunition and stockpiles. Nothing was left to chance. Even the weapons held by the Territorial Defence, or those that were still in the possession of the various factories and intended for the TO, these were weapons that were bought by the funds of the workers who produced them. These were all placed under the control of the JNA, with a view to fully disarming Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you agree that in the month of April, there were several attacks by Green Berets on Pretis? Some of them were successful and resulted in a large number of material and technical equipment and weapons being seized?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In any event, we need a year in the question. We just have "April."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: April of 1992, there were several successful attacks by the Green Berets on Pretis; yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I know of one successful attack, and I don't know that the Green Berets conducted the attack. Rather, it was the police special units. At the time, they seized a number of hand-held rocket-launchers, thankfully, because they were used to defend the Presidency in an attempt to carry out a coup on the top leadership in Skenderija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In early 1994, you transferred to the special-purpose industry, it is stated here, in your evidence in the case of General Milosevic on the 19th of February, 2007, page 2409, that you transferred to the special-purpose industry centre for manufacture of rifles and hand-grenades for the purposes of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: No, and I claim that I could not have stated this, because it's not the truth. It's not true that we manufactured rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about hand-grenades?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Hand-grenades, yes, and precisely out of the explosives I referred to earlier on. We exercised our primary inherent right to self-control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turkusic, I am not denying anyone's rights. I'm merely trying to establish facts. Did you, in Sarajevo, manufacture mortar shells as well?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have information to that effect. One needs to have a press and specialised technology to produce mortar shells. And although it was nearby in Vogosca, we didn't have it. As far as I know, not a single mortar shell was produced in Sarajevo, to the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mahmoud Cehajic, whom you know as deputy prime minister and a high functionary in the Party of Democratic Action -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know him personally, but I know who you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In his book, entitled War in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, at page 282, he says that in Sarajevo, a town as encircled as it was, some 40.000 mortar shells of the calibre of 82 millimetres was manufactured -- were manufactured. Is it possible to produce mortar shells with anything other than a press?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I would that this figure were true. I don't have knowledge to the effect that a single mortar shell was produced in Sarajevo, and I'm referring to the area of Sarajevo which was under siege. I am speaking here based on my memory and to the best of my knowledge. I cannot deny or challenge what someone says in his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. But will you agree that a shell can also be cast and not only used -- produced by a press?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, iron-casting is a very demanding job. We didn't have either the power or the requisite technology in Sarajevo to do that. Had this technology been used, I would have been informed of it, and I haven't been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. You were in that manufacturing centre. Is it true that your immediate supervisor was Farik Kulovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the capacity of some sort of a boss, there was also Veljko Zecevic; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The centre dealt with innovations, manufacture, and adjustment of material and technical equipment?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: We produced hand-grenades and rifle-launched grenades, and these were assets of a low explosive capacity. And that was the core production of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you produced these for the purposes of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which of the anti-aircraft defence systems were used by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: You mean "anti-aircraft," not "anti-air."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, PVO.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, none of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D2680 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fikret Prevljak was the commander of either the 1st Corps or the 12th Division; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I can see his signature here. If this is what a credible document states, then there's no need for me to confirm it. This is what the document reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at the first sentence, although I'll read it: "While touring the units of the 12th Division, it was established that fire positions for anti-aircraft and defence assets used for firing on the ground have not been done properly. In order to improve the situation, I hereby order as follows: "The fire positions which were erected for targeting targets on the ground should be further reinforced and fortified in order to fully guarantee the safety of those operating them and to enable prolonged combat activity." Under 2: "They should be fully camouflaged." Do you agree that this order was issued on the 23rd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That's the date that the document bears.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's right. And they hid this, they concealed this from you, did they?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't interesting enough for anyone to conceal things from me; to either inform me of them or to conceal them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the document admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see no basis to admit this through this witness, who said nothing about this document. How can you complain about shortage of time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that he did not see or observe the BH Army using air-bombs and anti-aircraft defence assets for targets on the ground, and this document proves the contrary. This document shows that they were fully masked and camouflaged so that no one would be able to detect them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll have another opportunity to tender this document, and then you can make your submission as to the credibility of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that afterwards, you took part in investigations, and that these investigations were just like in peacetime, except that they had undergone certain adjustments, they were adapted to a certain extent. Is that what you said? Can you tell us what it was that changed in relation to peacetime investigations?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, that's very simple. When the Department of Counter-Sabotage Protection, which exists in any police force in wartime and peacetime, does its work, they go to investigate situations when there are a large number of casualties, and then they go to investigate all the technical aspects involved with a particular incident and they apply their technical knowledge in order to carry out an on-site investigation that explains, in detail, what had happened, what the origin of the incident was, what the equipment was that caused loss of life and injury. If it was military equipment and if it was air-borne, it is only logical to look at the azimuth, the direction from where it had been fired, and everything else that pertains, in a technical sense, to the facts that may remain documented and archived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the point of view of criminal law, were your investigations more thorough or more superficial during the war?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, not in a single war can a police force --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, do not explain anything to us in general terms. What was the situation where we were?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "us"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, if you mean the KDZ where I was, they were a lot more thorough. We dealt with every little detail very seriously, a lot more seriously, and we did not want to record anything that we were not absolutely certain of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that is an answer, isn't it? Later on, you were appointed inspector for pyrotechnics. What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That meant a maximum level of knowledge and professionalism in a field that is relevant to the defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the application and development of pyrotechnics, what did that denote?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, that is, actually, what it says in the appointment when I was appointed to this position. When we collected unexploded ordnance, we actually took this apart, and I am not aware of that ever having happened before that in any war. We took out the explosive, once we removed the fuse, and then we handed it over for further processing for defence purposes. That was one of our tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which method did you use to extract the explosive?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I said already there are two ways of getting TNT out of this kind of a shell; using a high-temperature steam at 80 degrees, and then it melts and it literally drips like wax when a candle is burning. The other possibility is when it is hammered out. When stone is carved, for instance, you can compare it to that. However, it is important not to have any sparks, because that may cause a further explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you did that at the technical school; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I did not do that at the technical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So where did you do it?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: At the CMP, and at the KDZ later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where are these facilities, where are they located?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: CMP and then KDZ.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: CMP was at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering and the Faculty of Natural Sciences and Mathematics. It was by the very separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The KDZ?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: The KDZ was in Titova Street, Tito Street. That is the building of the federal MUP nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether any accidents happened at any one of these locations, and do you know that some young men got killed when a workshop exploded, some young men lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not at our location. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was at the technical school. So do you know which explosives were manufactured at Bosnalijek?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I have no information about that, absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, you spoke about the effect of coaxiality -- the effect of coaxiality on the montage of rocket engines as a factor of imprecision. On the basis of what did you establish that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I'm certain of that on the basis of the following fact: That placing rocket engines in an improvised manner, together with an air-bomb, can only be done in a very sophisticated plant where there are three-dimensional pieces of positioning equipment that are based on laser, for instance, just like what the aircraft manufacturing industry uses so that there is no mistake when engines are made. That is the way in which they were made, and that is -- what you call them in your documents, you call them make-shift devices. So from the point of view of parallel engines and the parallel bombs, the device can rotate. The trajectory can change immediately after it is launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But that is your position, but how did you actually establish that?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I know enough physics to be certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you knew that theoretically. So that is a theoretical assumption that you did not confirm on an unexploded bomb; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, unexploded ordnance would not be appropriate for confirming that. It would have been deformed if it had not exploded, so that would be an unreliable source for any kind of measurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you did not experiment, you did not do any research, you did not come to this conclusion on the basis of any kind of literature?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Literature about rocket -- rocket-propelled engines is something that we had at the KDZ. We knew about rockets. These are basic elements, that rocket engines that propel a bomb that weighs almost 300 kilometres [as interpreted] have to be absolutely symmetrically positioned with axes that are ideally parallel. That is more than clear. Even the smallest deviation of the axis of the engine in relation to others can lead to a change in the direction of the air-bomb and turn it into an imprecise piece of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that we had under our control Pretis, which was the best factory of special production. Did we also have under our control Oro in Rajlovac, which manufactured air equipment of the greatest possible precision?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection, sorry. I believe that the accused has not yet elicited evidence that this location in Rajlovac manufactured air equipment of the greatest possible precision. That's assuming a fact not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is assistance that is being given to the witness. He doesn't need any assistance. The witness knows what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The factory in Rajlovac, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But separate from this issue, I hoped that Judge Morrison's kind lecture would work. When would you come to the real questions? In relation to these issues, you can just put your case. Be more efficient. Think about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I am going to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turkusic, you are not right when you say that this is imprecisely mounted, because we had excellent factories in our hands and excellent experts. This was not done in a blacksmith store, in a car repair store. This was done in factories with sophisticated technology. Did we not have two such factories in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, you had the factory in Sarajevo. And if what you are saying is true, then you intentionally targeted Alipasino Polje, the most densely-populated area of Sarajevo, with a modified air-bomb. If you are saying that you were precise, then you did that intentionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Leave that aside. That is the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, we did not hear the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Because of overlapping, the interpreters couldn't hear you, Dr. Turkusic. After saying that, I quote: "If you are saying that you were precise, then you did that intentionally." Did you say something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said, If you were precise and if you claim that these modified air-bombs were very sophisticated, precise, manufactured in a modern factory, it is only a logical fact, then, and it is proof that the modified air-bomb targeted the most densely-populated area in the Balkans, perhaps, but certainly in Sarajevo. This bomb fell in Alipasino Polje, among buildings which were purely residential buildings, apartment buildings, so the logical conclusion is that you did it on purpose, if it is a precise piece of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turkusic, on the basis of such statements, the indictment charges us with having used ammunition that cannot be used. We say that that is not the case, and you said that also this lack of aerodynamic quality of this air-bomb contributes to its imprecision, and a sound is created, and therefore it is less precise. What about mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Mortar shells are highly aerodynamic, although they create a sound, and it is a well-known thing that in a war, if you hear the sound of a mortar shell, it will not kill you, but you do not hear the sound of the one that will kill you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, there are mistakes. It is probably because we speak so fast, but it is not right. Can it please be corrected through the audio-recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's go through this again, and then let's see how much time we have left. Did you investigate the incident in relation to the Holiday Inn on the 24th of November? It is a rocket-launcher 94; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Please remind me by using a document to jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This happened in Hamdije Cemerlica, which was formerly the street of Bratstvo-Jedinstvo; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Could the document please be shown to me to refresh my memory? This was 15 or 16 years ago. I don't know which date you mean.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2712, can we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this? Is that the incident?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: The first thing I see -- the first thing I see in this document is that what was sent to us from -- from us to the KDZ was this document from the ministry in Sarajevo, on the basis of which we compile a report. So the CSB addressed us, and so on, in relation to expert findings related to the explosion on the 24th of November, 1994, in the urban area of Sarajevo, and during the on-site investigation several metal pieces that were irregularly shaped were there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was submitted to us were these metal pieces that we were supposed to analyse, and the type of projectile was supposed to be established, and the direction from which they were fired. I cannot see the end, so I do not see what it says further on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear Mr. Karadzic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry. I just want to note for the record, Mr. President, that at the moment we're dealing with an incident which is not a part of the amalgamated statement of the witness and is not referred to in the indictment against the accused, just in terms of assessing the relevance of this line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's not in the indictment, and, actually, I'd like to give up on this. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As you confirmed today, did you work on the investigation of Markale 2, as it is known?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 14404, page 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that: You said today, Mr. Turkusic, that what happened often was that one shell would fall, and then after that, in order to increase the number of casualties, then another one would fall. Could you please give us incidents of this nature? Could you please list some of them?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really list them, nor can I refer to them in terms of the dates when they happened, but everyone who was in Sarajevo at the time will confirm to you that that happened very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often, and what were the incidents involved when there would be one shell, and then investigation would be carried out, and then another shell would fall?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: There were several such incidents at funerals, when the dead were being buried. One shell would fall. When people are trying to deal with those wounded, then another one would fall in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber where and when that happened.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that it's been 15 years now, I cannot say that on the basis of memory only. If you insist on that, it is very easy to come by this kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The transcript reflects what you are claiming, so I will insist, Mr. Turkusic. Did any investigator ever get killed by such a second shell?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this a record -- Higher Court in Sarajevo; right. Record on the shelling in the street of Mula Mustafe Baseskije number 64. Does this refer to Markale 2?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, at 1305 hours, and this is a record that was compiled by the Higher Court in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the shell fell at 1305 hours; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: According to many of the witnesses who were nearby at the time, that is the hour that is most frequently referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And your task in the investigation was to establish the direction and also to provide your expert opinion on the traces involved in the explosion; right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you start the on-site investigation? What was it that you found there on the spot? What did you find there on the spot, and when did you start the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: When I first testified before the break, I told you how I came to the site. I saw automobiles with bodies of the dead and wounded. I went to the market to buy some food. That was the centre for food exchanges in Sarajevo, generally speaking. When I saw what had happened, I returned to headquarters, I took what I needed for the on-site investigation, and I immediately went to the site, itself. That was the beginning of the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us try to describe this to the Trial Chamber now. You understood that something had fallen. Did you hear a single shell?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I've already said before the Trial Chamber and before the break that I was in a building from which the impact of the shell could not be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that you did say somewhere that you heard the shell, that you were on Titova Street, some 10 minutes or less away from the spot. Did you go to see what it was all about and then go back to fetch your instruments?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: No, we went to fetch our instruments only after we'd seen cars full of bodies, car trunks ajar with limbs sticking out. And as soon as a convoy of the first cars of the sort passed us by, we went to fetch our instruments and then attended the scene. And I could not have said anything else anywhere because it would not have been the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I let the first incident go, but in this case Mr. Karadzic has said that the witness previously testified that he did hear the impact of the shell while he was on Tito Street. Can Mr. Karadzic provide a reference to that, please? And I'd just like to note, for the record, Mr. Karadzic's earlier reference to a page number of the witness's evidence in the Dragomir Milosevic case does not, in fact, contain the passage that he claimed it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you give us the reference, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the end of business, I will find the reference. And if I don't inform you of it, we'll let it stand, but I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Turkusic, can you tell us: How many shells landed on that day in that zone?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: This one shell, which became part of history, in the very center, and four more of them fell on a square where there is a theatre to the south of that area, and there were two more that landed on a parking-lot. The four shells I mentioned did not result in any fatalities, and just as millions of others that landed elsewhere in Sarajevo and did not result in fatalities, it did not attract the attention of anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: What was the time-line according to which these shells landed?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I think that the shell that hit Markale was the first one, and then followed by the four. But there are reports on all these shells, and if one looks at the times of impact associated with them, one can reconstruct the time-line. At any rate, in a very short span of time, all five of them landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. And then you said that you saw that people were placed in cars in such a way that their limbs were sticking out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I saw a number of cars passing me by, and from the car boot, which was ajar, I could see limbs sticking out. And that was on my way to the base that I saw this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about passenger cars?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the sort of cars that we were able to see at the start of today's session. Any car that would pass me by; a Yugo, Golf, van, whatever the vehicle that happened to pass by would be immediately in the service of transporting casualties to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where it happens -- where would it so happen that people who have just been injured or wounded or killed would be actually stuck into a car that happens to pass by?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I can explain it by the monstrosity of the war. Taxi-drivers would use filtered oil, they would recycle it, they were cleanse it, and then use it again. So we were forced to make use of whatever we had. Where else would we have put these bodies, these people; ambulances? Well, whatever was on the move was a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In a special report from the Security Services Centre of Sarajevo, dated the 29th of August, 1995, page 9916, it is stated that the CSB was informed of the shelling at 11.30, which is an hour and a half before the shelling took place. How do you account for this?

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: In no way can I account for this. I have never seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The reference, 65 ter 009906 -- 65 ter 09906. An hour and a half before the explosion took place, the CSB knew that there was one or was about to be.

utterances.speaker: EMIR TURKUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you haven't shown me the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps we can call up the redacted version of this. The public redacted version is P1908, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have offered already the redacted version?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes -- actually, I beg your pardon, no, I'm not able to confirm we've done that. Pardon me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not yet. We'll not broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
